topics.name: Electrical resistance
topics.kicker: How strongly something opposes electric current · Measured in ohms
topics.briefing: Electrical resistance is how strongly something fights the flow of electric current, a bit like a narrow pipe slowing down water. In 1827, Georg Ohm showed that the voltage across a wire equals the current times its resistance, and the unit of resistance, the ohm, is named for him. Resistance turns electrical energy into heat, which is why a toaster’s coils glow red, while superconductors cooled to very low temperatures have no resistance at all.
topics.answerHtml: resistance (accept electrical resistance or resistors; prompt on impedance; do not accept “resistivity” or “conductance”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: An ideal ammeter has almost none of this quantity, so it does not change the current it measures, while an ideal voltmeter has an enormous amount of it. In ordinary metals, this quantity increases as the temperature rises.
tossups.r: Georg Ohm found that voltage equals current times this quantity. For 10 points, name this property, measured in ohms, that opposes the flow of electric current.

tossups.p: In 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes [“KAH-mer-ling ON-us”] found that this quantity suddenly dropped to zero in mercury cooled with liquid helium, the first sign of superconductivity. Long, thin wires have more of this quantity than short, thick wires made of the same metal.
tossups.r: Ohm’s law says that voltage equals current times this quantity. For 10 points, name this property, measured in ohms.

tossups.p: The Drude [“DROO-duh”] model explains this quantity as electrons bumping into a metal’s ions as they drift along. Rubber and plastic are used to coat electrical wires because they have an enormous amount of this quantity.
tossups.r: This quantity equals voltage divided by current. For 10 points, name this property, symbolized R and measured in ohms.

tossups.p: Samuel Hunter Christie invented a diamond-shaped circuit, later made famous by Charles Wheatstone, that finds an unknown amount of this quantity by balancing it against known amounts until a meter in the middle reads zero. In a series circuit, the total amount of this quantity is the sum of each part’s amount.
tossups.r: It is measured with an ohmmeter. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in ohms, which equals voltage divided by current.

tossups.p: Samuel Langley’s bolometer detects faint heat radiation by measuring tiny changes in this quantity in a blackened metal strip. The reciprocal of this quantity is called conductance and is measured in siemens [“SEE-menz”], a unit once called the “mho.”
tossups.r: That word is this quantity’s unit spelled backward. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in ohms, which equals voltage divided by current.

tossups.p: James Prescott Joule found that the heat given off by a wire each second equals the square of the current times this quantity. The glowing coils in a toaster and the filament of an old-fashioned light bulb heat up because of this quantity.
tossups.r: Ohm’s law relates it to voltage and current. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in ohms, that opposes the flow of electricity.

tossups.p: A small circuit part marked with brown, black, and red stripes has 1,000 units of this quantity, according to a color code. Joining two equal amounts of this quantity side by side, in parallel, cuts the total amount in half.
tossups.r: Georg Ohm showed that this quantity equals voltage divided by current. For 10 points, name this property measured in ohms.

tossups.p: Thermistors work as thermometers because this quantity in them changes sharply with temperature, and light sensors called photocells lose much of this quantity in bright light. Unlike metals, semiconductors usually have less of this quantity when they are heated.
tossups.r: It is measured in ohms. For 10 points, name this quantity that equals voltage divided by current, according to Ohm’s law.

tossups.p: A strain gauge measures how much an object stretches by tracking changes in this quantity, which rises when a wire is pulled longer and thinner. For a wire, this quantity equals a material property called rho times the wire’s length, divided by its cross-sectional area.
tossups.r: Superconductors have none of it. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in ohms, which opposes electric current.

tossups.p: Heating coils in toasters and hair dryers are usually made of nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium, because it has a high value of this quantity for its size and holds up well when red-hot. A German physicist’s 1827 book _The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically_ introduced a law relating current, voltage, and this quantity.
tossups.r: The unit of this quantity is symbolized by the Greek letter omega. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in ohms.

tossups.p: When several parts are joined in parallel, the reciprocal of their combined amount of this quantity equals the sum of the reciprocals of each part’s amount. Gustav Kirchhoff’s circuit laws help find this quantity for complicated networks.
tossups.r: Thin wires have more of it than thick ones. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured with an ohmmeter, that equals voltage divided by current.

tossups.p: Because a battery has some of this quantity inside it, the voltage at its terminals drops when it delivers a large current. Power companies send electricity at very high voltages so that less current flows, cutting the energy this quantity wastes as heat in long wires.
tossups.r: Copper wires have very little of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in ohms, that opposes electric current.

tossups.p: Tunnel diodes show a “negative differential” form of this quantity, in which the current drops as the voltage rises over a certain range. Parts whose current is not proportional to voltage, such as ordinary diodes, are called “non-ohmic.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals voltage divided by current and is measured in ohms.

tossups.p: Adjustable sources of this quantity called rheostats [“REE-oh-stats”] and potentiometers can dim lights or change the speed of a motor. In the water-pipe comparison for circuits, a narrow section of pipe stands for this quantity, while water pressure stands for voltage.
tossups.r: Superconductors have none of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in ohms, that opposes the flow of electric current.

tossups.p: Polygraph machines, often called lie detectors, record how this quantity in a person’s skin drops when the person sweats. At room temperature, a silver wire has less of this quantity than a same-sized wire of any other metal, with copper close behind.
tossups.r: An ohmmeter measures it, and Ohm’s law says voltage equals current times it. For 10 points, name this property measured in ohms.

clues.t: How strongly a material or circuit part opposes the flow of electric current
Measured in ohms, symbolized by the Greek capital letter omega (Ω)
Ohm’s law: voltage equals current times this quantity (V = IR)
Turns electrical energy into heat, making toaster coils and old light-bulb filaments glow
Superconductors have none of it below a critical temperature
In a series circuit, the amounts simply add: total = R1 + R2 + …
In parallel, 1/total = 1/R1 + 1/R2, so two equal parts side by side give half the amount
Grows with a wire’s length and shrinks with its thickness: R = resistivity (rho) × length ÷ area
Rises with temperature in metals but usually falls when semiconductors are heated
Its reciprocal is conductance, measured in siemens (once called the “mho,” which is “ohm” spelled backward)
Small circuit parts that supply it are marked with colored bands; brown-black-red means 1,000 ohms
Heat given off each second = current squared × this quantity (Joule’s law), so power lines use high voltage and low current
Symbolized R; measured with an ohmmeter or a multimeter
At room temperature, a silver wire has less of it than a same-sized wire of any other metal; copper is close behind and is the usual wire metal
1911: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes saw it vanish in mercury cooled by liquid helium
An ideal ammeter has almost none of it and an ideal voltmeter has an enormous amount, so neither one disturbs the circuit
A Wheatstone bridge (invented by Samuel Hunter Christie) finds an unknown value by balancing until a meter reads zero
Georg Ohm published his law in _The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically_ (1827)
Insulators like rubber and plastic coat electrical wires because they have an enormous amount of it
The Drude model explains it as drifting electrons bumping into a metal’s ions
Thermistors change it sharply with temperature; light sensors called photocells lose much of it in bright light
Strain gauges measure stretching from changes in it as a wire gets longer and thinner
A battery’s “internal” amount makes its terminal voltage drop when it delivers a large current
Tunnel diodes show “negative differential” behavior: current falls as voltage rises over a certain range
Adjustable versions called rheostats and potentiometers can dim lights or change a motor’s speed
Samuel Langley’s bolometer detects faint heat radiation from tiny changes in it in a blackened metal strip
Heating coils are made of nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium with a high value of it for its size
Polygraphs (lie detectors) record how the skin’s amount drops when a person sweats

trap.title: Resistance or resistivity?
trap.body: Resistance belongs to one particular object, like a single wire or circuit part, while resistivity is a property of the material itself, no matter its size or shape. A long, thin copper wire has more resistance than a short, thick one, but both have the same resistivity. Conductance is the flip side: it is the reciprocal of resistance and is measured in siemens.
trap.fix: Ohms, Ohm’s law, V = IR, or “series and parallel” clues mean resistance. Units of ohm-meters, or “a property of the material,” point to resistivity; siemens or “reciprocal” points to conductance.
trap.line: Real answer line: resistance (accept electrical resistance or resistors; prompt on impedance; do not accept “resistivity” or “conductance”)

topics.name: Weak nuclear force
topics.kicker: Fundamental force behind beta decay · Carried by the W and Z bosons
topics.dates: First theory by Enrico Fermi, 1933; W and Z bosons found 1983
topics.briefing: The weak nuclear force is one of nature’s four fundamental forces, and it is the only one that can turn one type of quark into another, which is how a neutron becomes a proton in beta decay. It also starts the chain of fusion that makes the Sun shine. Its carrier particles, the heavy W and Z bosons, were discovered at CERN in 1983.
topics.answerHtml: weak nuclear force (accept weak interaction or weak force; prompt on electroweak interaction or nuclear force; do not accept “strong nuclear force”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1956, Chien-Shiung Wu [“chyen-SHYOONG WOO”] cooled radioactive cobalt-60 nuclei and found that their electrons shot out more often in one direction, proving that this force does not treat mirror images alike. Her result confirmed a prediction made by Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force, carried by W and Z bosons, that causes beta decay.

tossups.p: The Gargamelle bubble chamber at CERN found the first evidence of this force’s “neutral currents” in 1973. Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for a theory uniting this force with electromagnetism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force that causes radioactive beta decay and acts only over tiny distances.

tossups.p: Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer won a Nobel Prize after experiments at CERN found the particles that carry this force in 1983. Because those carrier particles are so heavy, this force reaches only across distances smaller than a proton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force that turns neutrons into protons in beta decay.

tossups.p: The journal _Nature_ rejected Enrico Fermi’s first theory of this force as too far removed from reality. That theory pictured four particles meeting at a single point and explained how a neutron can turn into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force, carried by W and Z bosons, which causes beta decay.

tossups.p: A matrix named for Cabibbo [“kuh-BEE-boh”], Kobayashi, and Maskawa describes how strongly this force mixes different kinds of quarks. Through this force, a down quark can change into an up quark by giving off a charged carrier particle, which turns a neutron into a proton.
tossups.r: Its W and Z carriers were found at CERN in 1983. For 10 points, name this fundamental force responsible for beta decay.

tossups.p: James Cronin and Val Fitch won a Nobel Prize for showing that decays of neutral kaons caused by this force break a symmetry called CP. This force is the only fundamental interaction known to violate parity, treating a process and its mirror image differently.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force that is stronger than gravity but much feebler than electromagnetism.

tossups.p: The Sun can shine for billions of years partly because the first step of its proton-proton chain needs this force to turn a proton into a neutron, which happens very rarely. This force also makes carbon-14 decay into nitrogen-14, the process behind radiocarbon dating.
tossups.r: It causes beta decay. For 10 points, name this fundamental force carried by the W and Z bosons.

tossups.p: The Higgs mechanism explains why the particles that carry this force have mass while the photon does not. Because those carriers are more than 80 times as heavy as a proton, this force acts only over tiny distances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force involved in beta decay, carried by the W and Z bosons.

tossups.p: One kind of particle that carries this force interacts only with “left-handed” matter particles, so this force can tell a process apart from its mirror image. This force changes the flavor of quarks and leptons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that makes a neutron decay into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino.

tossups.p: In the extremely hot early universe, this force and electromagnetism behaved as one single force, which later split apart as the universe cooled. This force is the only one that can change one flavor of quark into another.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force, which causes beta decay and is carried by the W and Z bosons.

tossups.p: Muons decay through this force in about two millionths of a second, producing an electron, a neutrino, and an antineutrino. A free neutron outside an atom’s nucleus lasts only about 15 minutes on average before this force makes it decay.
tossups.r: It causes beta decay. For 10 points, name this fundamental force carried by the W and Z bosons.

tossups.p: In electron capture, this force lets a proton in a nucleus absorb one of the atom’s inner electrons and become a neutron. Positron emission, also called beta-plus decay, is caused by this force as well.
tossups.r: Its carriers are the W and Z bosons. For 10 points, name this fundamental force responsible for all types of beta decay.

tossups.p: The strength of this force at low energies is set by the Fermi coupling constant, named for the scientist who wrote the first theory of it. Neutrinos are so hard to detect because, apart from gravity, this is the only force they feel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force, carried by W and Z bosons, that causes beta decay.

tossups.p: Charged pions decay into muons and neutrinos through this force, while neutral pions decay into gamma rays through electromagnetism instead. This force acts only over distances much smaller than an atomic nucleus, because its carrier particles are very heavy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force that causes beta decay, the second-feeblest of the four fundamental forces.

tossups.p: The “tau-theta puzzle,” in which two seemingly identical particles decayed in two different ways, led Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang to suggest that this force might not treat mirror images the same way. They won the 1957 Nobel Prize after that idea was confirmed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fundamental force, carried by W and Z bosons, that causes beta decay.

clues.t: One of the four fundamental forces, along with gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong force
Causes beta decay, in which a neutron turns into a proton and gives off an electron and an antineutrino
Carried by the W and Z bosons
Stronger than gravity but far feebler than electromagnetism and the strong force
Acts only over tiny distances, smaller than a proton, because its carrier particles are so heavy
The only force that can change one flavor of quark into another, such as a down quark into an up quark
Apart from gravity, the only force neutrinos feel, which is why they are so hard to detect
Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg united it with electromagnetism (Nobel Prize, 1979)
Its W and Z carriers were discovered at CERN in 1983; Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer won the 1984 Nobel Prize
Needed for the first step of the Sun’s proton-proton chain, when a proton turns into a neutron
Enrico Fermi wrote the first theory of it in 1933, to explain beta decay
Violates parity: it treats a process and its mirror image differently
Makes carbon-14 decay into nitrogen-14, the basis of radiocarbon dating
The Higgs mechanism gives its W and Z carriers mass, while the photon stays massless
1956: Chien-Shiung Wu’s cobalt-60 experiment proved that it violates parity
Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang predicted its parity violation to solve the “tau-theta puzzle” (Nobel Prize, 1957)
The Gargamelle bubble chamber at CERN found its “neutral currents” in 1973
James Cronin and Val Fitch found CP violation in its decays of neutral kaons (1964)
The CKM (Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa) matrix describes how it mixes different kinds of quarks
The journal _Nature_ rejected Fermi’s theory of it, which pictured four particles meeting at a single point
Its W carriers interact only with “left-handed” matter particles
In the hot early universe, it and electromagnetism acted as one single force
Muons decay through it in about two millionths of a second, into an electron, a neutrino, and an antineutrino
A free neutron outside a nucleus decays through it in about 15 minutes on average
Also causes electron capture and positron emission (beta-plus decay)
Its strength at low energies is set by the Fermi coupling constant
Charged pions decay into muons and neutrinos through it; neutral pions decay through electromagnetism instead

trap.title: Weak or strong force?
trap.body: Both are called nuclear forces, and both act only over tiny distances about the size of a nucleus or smaller, so their clues can sound alike. The strong force, carried by gluons, holds quarks together and binds protons and neutrons into a nucleus; this force, carried by the W and Z bosons, makes particles change identity and causes beta decay. Answering just “nuclear force” is not enough.
trap.fix: W or Z bosons, beta decay, neutrinos, parity violation, or changing quark flavors means the weak force. Gluons, color charge, or holding a nucleus together means the strong force.
trap.line: Real answer line: weak nuclear force (accept weak interaction or weak force; prompt on electroweak interaction or nuclear force; do not accept “strong nuclear force”)

topics.name: Scattering
topics.kicker: Light and particles bouncing off in new directions · Why the sky is blue
topics.dates: Rayleigh explained the blue sky in 1871
topics.briefing: Scattering happens when light or a particle hits something and bounces off in a new direction. Air molecules scatter blue sunlight much more than red, which is why the sky looks blue and sunsets glow orange and red. Physicists also scatter particles off targets to study things too small to see: alpha particles bouncing back from thin gold foil led Ernest Rutherford to discover the atomic nucleus in 1911.
topics.answerHtml: scattering (accept word forms like scatter; accept specific types like Rayleigh scattering or Compton scattering; prompt on Tyndall effect, Compton effect, or Raman effect; do not accept “diffraction”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In one type of this process, the amount of light affected goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power, so short blue waves are affected far more than long red ones. This process also explains why sunsets glow orange and red.
tossups.r: That type is named for Lord Rayleigh. For 10 points, name this process in which air molecules send sunlight off in all directions, making the sky look blue.

tossups.p: C. V. Raman began studying this process after wondering why the Mediterranean Sea looked so blue during a 1921 sea voyage. In 1928, he found an “inelastic” form of this process, in which light comes out with a slightly different wavelength.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that Lord Rayleigh used to explain the blue color of the sky.

tossups.p: Arthur Compton won a Nobel Prize for showing that X-rays bounce off electrons like billiard balls in this process, coming out with longer wavelengths. That 1923 result helped convince physicists that light comes in particles called photons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that, for sunlight in air, makes the daytime sky look blue.

tossups.p: Gustav Mie [“MEE”] worked out the math of this process for particles as large as a light wave or larger, which explains why the water droplets in clouds look white instead of blue. Smaller particles, like air molecules, favor blue light in this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes the daytime sky blue and sunsets red.

tossups.p: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil and saw a few of them bounce almost straight back, an example of this process. Ernest Rutherford used the result to discover the tiny, dense atomic nucleus in 1911.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which waves or particles are knocked into new directions, which makes the sky look blue.

tossups.p: At SLAC in the late 1960s, “deep inelastic” experiments of this kind, which fired electrons at protons, revealed that protons are made of smaller particles later identified as quarks. Physicists describe how likely this process is with a quantity called a cross section.
tossups.r: In the air, this process sends blue sunlight in all directions. For 10 points, name this process that makes the sky look blue.

tossups.p: The likelihood of this process is often measured in a tiny unit of area called the barn, which got its name from the joke that a uranium nucleus was “as big as a barn.” On Mars, fine dust in the air causes this process to make sunsets look blue.
tossups.r: On Earth, this process by air molecules makes the daytime sky blue. For 10 points, name this process, in which light is redirected after hitting particles.

tossups.p: John Tyndall [“TIN-dul”] showed that a light beam becomes visible as it passes through a colloid, such as milky water or fog, because tiny particles cause this process. Clouds look white because their water droplets cause this process for all colors about equally.
tossups.r: Air molecules send blue sunlight in all directions in this process. For 10 points, name this process that makes the sky look blue.

tossups.p: Sunlight that undergoes this process in the sky becomes partly polarized, most strongly in directions at right angles to the Sun, and bees use that pattern to navigate. This process affects violet light even more than blue light, but sunlight contains less violet and human eyes are more sensitive to blue.
tossups.r: That is why this process makes the sky look blue, not violet. For 10 points, name this process, which also makes sunsets red.

tossups.p: Blue eyes contain no blue pigment; instead, they get their color from this process in a layer of the iris. This process in the air between you and a faraway mountain range makes the mountains look hazy and bluish.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process by which air molecules redirect sunlight, making the daytime sky blue.

tossups.p: Before neutral atoms formed, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, light could not travel far because of the Thomson type of this process, in which light bounces off free electrons without losing energy. That type is the low-energy version of a type named for Arthur Compton.
tossups.r: In air, this process favors blue light. For 10 points, name this process that makes the daytime sky look blue.

tossups.p: In some smoke detectors, smoke particles send part of a light beam onto a sensor by this process, setting off the alarm. Types of this process that change the light’s energy, like Raman’s, are called inelastic, while types that do not, like Rayleigh’s, are called elastic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which makes the sky look blue and clouds look white.

tossups.p: A formula named for Ernest Rutherford predicts that the number of alpha particles sent off at an angle by this process drops sharply as that angle grows, following one over the sine of half the angle to the fourth power. That formula matched the results of the gold foil experiment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which particles or waves are deflected after hitting something, the reason the sky looks blue.

tossups.p: In the “inverse” form of a type of this process named for Arthur Compton, fast-moving electrons give energy to low-energy photons, boosting them to X-ray or gamma-ray energies. Raman spectroscopy uses this process to identify molecules from the tiny wavelength shifts they give to laser light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes the daytime sky look blue and sunsets look red.

tossups.p: Astronauts on the Moon saw a black sky even in full sunlight, because the Moon has almost no air to cause this process. Lord Rayleigh used this process in 1871 to explain a color that people see every day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which air molecules redirect sunlight, making the sky blue.

clues.t: Light or particles hit something and bounce off in new directions
Air molecules send blue sunlight off in all directions, making the daytime sky look blue
Sunsets look red and orange because blue light is removed along the long path through the air
Lord Rayleigh explained the blue sky with it in 1871
Rutherford’s gold foil experiment bounced alpha particles off atoms, revealing the nucleus
Rayleigh’s type depends on 1 ÷ wavelength to the fourth power, so short blue waves are affected most
Gustav Mie’s type, by particles as big as a light wave or bigger, affects all colors about equally, so clouds look white
Arthur Compton (1923): X-rays bounce off electrons and come out with longer wavelengths, showing light acts as particles (photons)
C. V. Raman (Nobel Prize, 1930) found an “inelastic” type in which light’s wavelength shifts slightly
The Tyndall effect: tiny particles in a colloid or in fog make a light beam visible
Violet is affected even more than blue, but sunlight has less violet and our eyes are more sensitive to blue
Blue eyes have no blue pigment; their color comes from it in a layer of the iris
Elastic types (like Rayleigh’s) keep the light’s energy; inelastic types (like Raman’s) change it
Skylight is partly polarized by it, most strongly at right angles to the Sun; bees navigate using the pattern
Faraway mountains look hazy and bluish because of it in the air in between
Raman got curious on a 1921 sea voyage, wondering why the Mediterranean Sea was so blue; India’s National Science Day (February 28) honors his discovery
Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden did the gold foil experiment (1909); Rutherford explained it in 1911
Rutherford’s formula: the number sent off at an angle falls as 1 ÷ the sine of half the angle to the fourth power
SLAC’s “deep inelastic” experiments (late 1960s) fired electrons at protons and found quarks inside
Its likelihood is a “cross section,” measured in barns (a uranium nucleus was joked to be “as big as a barn”)
Thomson’s type is light bouncing off free electrons without losing energy, the low-energy version of Compton’s
Before neutral atoms formed, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, it off free electrons kept light from traveling far
On Mars, fine dust in the air makes sunsets look blue
In some smoke detectors, smoke particles send part of a light beam onto a sensor by it, setting off the alarm
In “inverse” Compton’s type, fast electrons boost low-energy photons up to X-ray or gamma-ray energies
Raman spectroscopy identifies molecules from the tiny wavelength shifts they give to laser light
Astronauts on the Moon saw a black sky even in sunlight, because there is almost no air there to cause it

trap.title: Not diffraction or refraction
trap.body: Scattering, diffraction, refraction, and reflection are all things light can do, and quiz bowl treats them as separate answers. Scattering sends light off in many directions after it hits small particles, like air molecules (the blue sky) or the atoms in gold foil. Diffraction is a wave spreading around an edge or through a narrow slit, refraction is light bending as it enters a new material, and reflection is bouncing off a surface like a mirror.
trap.fix: Blue sky, sunsets, colloids, Compton, Raman, or gold foil means scattering, and specific types like “Rayleigh scattering” are fine. Slits or gratings mean diffraction, prisms or lenses mean refraction, and saying just “Lord Rayleigh” names the scientist, not the process.
trap.line: Real answer line: scattering (accept word forms like scatter; accept specific types like Rayleigh scattering or Compton scattering; prompt on Tyndall effect, Compton effect, or Raman effect; do not accept “diffraction”)

topics.name: Uncertainty principle
topics.kicker: Heisenberg’s quantum limit · Exact position or exact momentum, never both
topics.briefing: In 1927, a 25-year-old German physicist named Werner Heisenberg found a strange rule of the quantum world: the more exactly you know where a tiny particle like an electron is, the less exactly you can know its momentum, and the reverse. This isn’t because our tools are clumsy; the limit is built into nature, because particles also behave like waves. It even helps explain why atoms don’t collapse.
topics.answerHtml: uncertainty principle (accept Heisenberg uncertainty principle or indeterminacy principle; prompt on Heisenberg or uncertainty)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Earle Kennard proved this principle’s modern form, in which the spreads in a particle’s position and momentum multiply to at least h-bar over two. This principle shows that electrons cannot follow the exact circular orbits of the Bohr model.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of quantum mechanics, stated by Werner Heisenberg in 1927.

tossups.p: In a famous thought experiment, trying to pinpoint an electron with a microscope that uses very short-wavelength gamma rays gives the electron an unpredictable kick, illustrating this principle. This principle applies to pairs of quantities called conjugate variables.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle formulated by Werner Heisenberg, which says a particle’s position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

tossups.p: At the 1930 Solvay Conference, Albert Einstein described a box that releases a single photon at a precisely known time, hoping to beat the energy-time form of this principle. Niels Bohr answered him using Einstein’s own theory of general relativity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, discovered by Werner Heisenberg, which says position and momentum cannot both be measured precisely.

tossups.p: Because of this principle, a trapped particle can never be perfectly still, so it always keeps some “zero-point energy,” which helps explain why helium stays liquid near absolute zero unless it is squeezed under high pressure. This principle is a basic rule of nature, not a limit of clumsy measuring tools.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle by Werner Heisenberg, which says you cannot know both a particle’s exact position and its exact momentum.

tossups.p: Atoms in short-lived excited states give off spectral lines with a “natural width” instead of a perfectly sharp color because of one form of this principle. That form links the spread in a state’s energy to how long the state lasts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum principle, which says that a particle’s position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

tossups.p: Mathematically, this principle follows from the fact that a wave packet squeezed into a small region must be built from many different wavelengths, a property of Fourier transforms. It holds because particles like electrons also behave like waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, stated by Werner Heisenberg, that limits how precisely position and momentum can be known together.

tossups.p: The LIGO gravitational-wave detectors use “squeezed light” to cut noise, making one property of the light more precise at the cost of another, without breaking this principle. This principle’s limit is set by the reduced Planck constant, h-bar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, which says a particle’s position and momentum can’t both be pinned down exactly.

tossups.p: Shrinking the width of a single slit makes the electrons passing through it spread out more widely on a screen, a result that matches this principle. Pinning down where each electron crossed the slit makes its sideways momentum harder to predict.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle discovered by Werner Heisenberg in 1927, which limits how well position and momentum can be known.

tossups.p: This principle follows from the fact that two quantum operators, x and p, do not commute: their commutator equals i times h-bar. The scientist behind this principle developed matrix mechanics with Max Born and Pascual Jordan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that limits how precisely a particle’s position and momentum can be known together.

tossups.p: This principle helps explain why an electron does not crash into an atom’s nucleus, since squeezing the electron into a tiny space would give it a huge spread of momentum and a lot of energy. It applies to pairs of quantities called conjugate variables.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of Werner Heisenberg, which says a particle’s exact position and momentum can’t both be known.

tossups.p: Hideki Yukawa’s prediction of a particle carrying the force that holds atomic nuclei together is often explained with one form of this principle, which allows short-lived “virtual” particles to briefly pop into existence. That form relates energy and time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, formulated by Werner Heisenberg, stating that position and momentum cannot both be measured exactly.

tossups.p: Niels Bohr linked this principle to his idea of complementarity, which says that wave and particle pictures are both needed but can never be used at the same time. Both ideas became part of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, published by Werner Heisenberg in 1927, about measuring position and momentum.

tossups.p: In signal processing, the Gabor [“GAH-bor”] limit is a version of this principle: a sound that lasts only an instant cannot have a precise pitch, and a pure pitch must last a long time. This principle is not the same as the observer effect, in which measuring something disturbs it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle by Werner Heisenberg, which says position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

tossups.p: A 25-year-old physicist worked out this principle in early 1927 while working at Niels Bohr’s institute in Copenhagen. That physicist had already helped create matrix mechanics, and he won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: That physicist was Werner Heisenberg. For 10 points, name this principle about the limits of measuring position and momentum.

tossups.p: Richard Feynman wrote that this principle protects quantum mechanics, because any device that tells which slit each electron passes through in the double-slit experiment wipes out the interference pattern. This principle says the spreads in position and momentum multiply to at least h-bar over two.
tossups.r: It was stated by Werner Heisenberg in 1927. For 10 points, name this principle of quantum mechanics.

clues.t: The more exactly you know a particle’s position, the less exactly you can know its momentum, and the reverse
Stated by the German physicist Werner Heisenberg in 1927
In symbols: delta x times delta p is at least h-bar over 2
A basic rule of quantum mechanics, not a problem with clumsy measuring tools
A second form links energy and time: a state that lasts only briefly has a spread-out energy
Comes from particles acting like waves: a wave squeezed into a small space must mix many wavelengths
Applies to pairs of conjugate variables, like position and momentum
Its limit is set by the reduced Planck constant, h-bar (h divided by 2π)
Not the same as the observer effect: the limit exists even with perfect instruments
Narrowing a single slit makes the electrons passing through it spread out more on a screen
Helps explain why electrons don’t crash into the nucleus: squeezing one into a tiny space would give it lots of energy
Gamma-ray microscope thought experiment: seeing an electron gives it an unpredictable kick
Heisenberg worked it out in early 1927, at age 25, at Niels Bohr’s institute in Copenhagen
Earle Kennard proved its modern form, using standard deviations and h-bar over 2
Shows that electrons cannot follow the exact circular orbits of the Bohr model
The position and momentum operators don’t commute: their commutator equals i times h-bar
At the 1930 Solvay Conference, Einstein’s photon box tried to beat it; Bohr answered with general relativity
Bohr tied it to his complementarity idea in the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics
A trapped particle is never perfectly still (zero-point energy), which helps keep helium liquid near absolute zero
Short-lived excited states give spectral lines a natural width instead of a perfectly sharp color
Follows mathematically from Fourier transforms of wave packets
The Gabor limit in signal processing: a sound that lasts only an instant can’t have a precise pitch
LIGO uses “squeezed light,” making one property of light more precise at the cost of another
Used to explain short-lived “virtual” particles and Hideki Yukawa’s prediction of a particle that holds atomic nuclei together
Heisenberg helped create matrix mechanics with Max Born and Pascual Jordan, and won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics
Richard Feynman wrote that it protects quantum mechanics: finding which slit an electron used wipes out the interference pattern

trap.title: Not the observer effect
trap.body: People often describe this principle as “measuring something disturbs it,” but that idea is the observer effect. Heisenberg’s principle goes deeper: there is a basic limit to how precisely position and momentum can both be known, even with perfect instruments, because particles behave like waves. Quiz bowl also has separate answer lines for the Pauli exclusion principle (no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers) and Bohr’s complementarity.
trap.fix: Position and momentum, energy and time, h-bar over 2, or Heisenberg means the uncertainty principle. Two electrons, quantum numbers, or orbitals filling up means the Pauli exclusion principle; saying just “Heisenberg” earns only a prompt, so add “uncertainty principle.”
trap.line: Real answer line: uncertainty principle (accept Heisenberg uncertainty principle or indeterminacy principle; prompt on Heisenberg or uncertainty)

topics.name: Electric field
topics.kicker: Force per unit charge around every charge · Mapped with lines of force
topics.dates: Lines of force pictured by Michael Faraday, 1800s
topics.briefing: An electric field is the invisible zone of push and pull that surrounds every electric charge. Michael Faraday pictured it as lines that point away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and the closer together the lines, the stronger the field. A balloon rubbed on your hair tugs on it through its electric field, and sharks can sense the faint electric fields made by the muscles of hidden prey.
topics.answerHtml: electric field (accept E-field or electrostatic field; prompt on field or electromagnetic field; do not accept “magnetic field”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Johannes Stark won a Nobel Prize for discovering that this quantity splits the spectral lines of atoms. Inside a closed metal box called a Faraday cage, this quantity is zero, which shields anything inside from outside charges.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vector quantity, measured in newtons per coulomb, that equals the force on a charge divided by the charge.

tossups.p: Gauss’s law says that the flux of this quantity through any closed surface equals the charge inside divided by the permittivity of free space. Lines showing this quantity begin on positive charges and end on negative charges.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the force per unit charge at each point around a charged object.

tossups.p: Robert Millikan measured the charge of a single electron by adjusting this quantity between two metal plates until tiny charged oil drops hung motionless in midair. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, this quantity is nearly the same everywhere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in volts per meter or newtons per coulomb.

tossups.p: This quantity equals the negative gradient of the voltage, so it points “downhill” from high voltage toward low voltage. Lines showing this quantity always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, and they never cross each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

tossups.p: When this quantity reaches about three million volts per meter, dry air breaks down and conducts, letting a spark jump across a gap. An electron placed in this quantity is pushed in the direction opposite to the way this quantity points.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the force per unit charge, that surrounds every charged object.

tossups.p: In gel electrophoresis [“ih-lek-troh-fuh-REE-sis”], scientists use this quantity to pull DNA fragments through a gel, sorting them by size. Any charged particle placed in this quantity feels a force equal to its charge times the strength of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity found by dividing the force on a small test charge by the size of that charge.

tossups.p: Sharks use jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini to sense faint versions of this quantity given off by the muscles of hidden prey. Platypuses can also sense this quantity with their bills while hunting underwater with their eyes closed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which points away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

tossups.p: The strength of this quantity around a dipole falls off with the cube of the distance, faster than around a single point charge. Around a point charge, Coulomb’s law says this quantity falls off with the square of the distance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vector quantity, which can be drawn as lines of force around any charge.

tossups.p: According to Faraday’s law of induction, a changing magnetic field creates a curling version of this quantity. Light is a wave made of this quantity and a magnetic partner that vibrate at right angles to each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose SI units are newtons per coulomb, the force per unit charge.

tossups.p: The metal dome of a Van de Graaff generator builds up enough charge to create a strong version of this quantity, which can make a person’s hair stand on end. Charge on a conductor crowds onto sharp points, making this quantity strongest there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that tells how a charge would be pushed or pulled at each point in space.

tossups.p: The energy stored per cubic meter in a region with this quantity equals one-half the permittivity of free space times this quantity squared. Dielectric materials placed in this quantity become polarized, which reduces this quantity inside them.
tossups.r: Capacitors store energy in this quantity. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in volts per meter.

tossups.p: In 1897, J. J. Thomson bent cathode rays using this quantity and a magnetic one to find the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron. Oscilloscope tubes once steered their electron beams with plates that created this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that points away from positive charges and toward negative charges.

tossups.p: Around a very large flat sheet of charge, this quantity has the same strength at every distance, while around a long charged wire, it weakens in proportion to one over the distance. A small positive test charge is used to map this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the force per unit charge, which Michael Faraday drew as lines of force.

tossups.p: Linear particle accelerators, like the two-mile-long machine at SLAC, use oscillating versions of this quantity to speed up electrons. In a uniform version of this quantity, a charged particle speeds up steadily, just as a falling ball does in gravity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in newtons per coulomb, whose lines Michael Faraday drew around charges.

tossups.p: St. Elmo’s fire glows on ship masts and airplane wings during storms when this quantity becomes very strong around pointed objects. This quantity is strongest wherever the lines that represent it are packed closest together.
tossups.r: Its SI unit is the newton per coulomb. For 10 points, name this quantity, the force per unit charge, which surrounds every charged object.

clues.t: The force a charge would feel at each point in space, divided by the size of that charge (force per unit charge)
Measured in newtons per coulomb, which is the same as volts per meter
Points away from positive charges and toward negative charges
Drawn as lines of force, an idea from Michael Faraday; closer lines mean a stronger push
Made by charges, even ones sitting still; its magnetic partner comes from moving charges and magnets
Around a point charge it follows Coulomb’s law, falling off with the square of the distance
A charge placed in it feels a force equal to the charge times its strength (F = qE)
Zero inside a closed metal shell (a Faraday cage) or inside any conductor whose charges are at rest
Nearly uniform between two oppositely charged parallel plates, as in a capacitor
Points “downhill” from high voltage to low; it equals the negative gradient of the voltage
Light is a wave of it and its magnetic partner, vibrating at right angles to each other
Gauss’s law: its flux through a closed surface equals the charge inside divided by the permittivity of free space
Sharks (using ampullae of Lorenzini) and platypuses can sense faint ones made by hidden prey
The Stark effect: it splits atoms’ spectral lines (Johannes Stark, Nobel Prize 1919)
Robert Millikan balanced charged oil drops in it to measure the electron’s charge
Dry air breaks down and sparks when it reaches about 3 million volts per meter
Around a dipole it falls off with the cube of the distance
Gel electrophoresis uses it to pull DNA fragments through a gel and sort them by size
J. J. Thomson bent cathode rays with it (and a magnetic one) to find the electron’s charge-to-mass ratio in 1897
Energy stored per cubic meter = ½ × the permittivity of free space × its strength squared
Same strength at any distance from a huge flat sheet of charge; falls as 1/r around a long charged wire
Its lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles and never cross each other
Faraday’s law of induction: a changing magnetic field creates a curling version of it
A Van de Graaff generator makes a strong one that can make hair stand on end; it is strongest near sharp points
Dielectric materials become polarized in it, which reduces it inside them
Linear accelerators like SLAC’s two-mile machine use oscillating ones to speed up electrons
St. Elmo’s fire glows on ship masts and airplane wings when it gets very strong around pointed objects

trap.title: Electric or magnetic?
trap.body: Electric and magnetic fields are partners (light is a wave of both), and quiz bowl has separate answer lines for each. Charges make an electric field even when they sit still, and it pushes on any charge, moving or not; a magnetic field comes from moving charges or magnets, and it pushes only on charges that are moving. Some tossups instead want related answers like electric potential (voltage) or electric flux.
trap.fix: Newtons per coulomb, volts per meter, Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s law, the Stark effect, or Millikan’s oil drops means electric field. Teslas, compass needles, the right-hand rule, the Hall effect, or the Zeeman effect means magnetic field.
trap.line: Real answer line: electric field (accept E-field or electrostatic field; prompt on field or electromagnetic field; do not accept “magnetic field”)

topics.name: Neutrinos
topics.kicker: Nearly massless “ghost particles” · Trillions pass through you every second
topics.dates: Proposed by Wolfgang Pauli, 1930; first detected 1956
topics.briefing: Neutrinos are tiny particles with no electric charge and almost no mass, and they barely interact with anything, so trillions of them stream through your body every second without a trace. Wolfgang Pauli proposed them in 1930 to explain where energy seemed to vanish in radioactive beta decay, but they weren’t detected until 1956. Scientists catch them with giant tanks of water deep underground, or with a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole.
topics.answerHtml: neutrinos (accept specific types like electron neutrinos or antineutrinos; prompt on leptons; do not accept “neutrons”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 2011, the OPERA experiment reported measurements suggesting that these particles traveled from CERN to a lab in Italy faster than light, but the result was traced to a loose fiber-optic cable. These particles are leptons, like the electron and the muon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these nearly massless, electrically neutral particles first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli.

tossups.p: Ray Davis used a huge tank of dry-cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota gold mine to catch these particles from the Sun, but found only about a third as many as John Bahcall had predicted. That shortfall was explained when scientists learned these particles change type as they travel.
tossups.r: Trillions of them pass through your body every second. For 10 points, name these ghostly, nearly massless particles that stream out of the Sun.

tossups.p: Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines first detected these particles in 1956, using tanks of water placed near a nuclear reactor at the Savannah River plant in South Carolina. Reines shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics for that discovery.
tossups.r: These particles barely interact with matter. For 10 points, name these tiny, electrically neutral particles given off in beta decay.

tossups.p: Wolfgang Pauli first proposed these particles in a 1930 letter that began “Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen,” calling his idea a “desperate remedy” to save the conservation of energy. He called them “neutrons,” a name later given to a much heavier particle found by James Chadwick in 1932.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles, which are given off along with electrons in beta decay.

tossups.p: About two dozen of these particles from Supernova 1987A were caught by detectors in Japan, the United States, and the Soviet Union, arriving hours before the exploding star’s light was seen. Masatoshi Koshiba shared the 2002 Nobel Prize for detecting them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these nearly massless particles, which come in electron, muon, and tau flavors.

tossups.p: In 1998, the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan found that these particles, made when cosmic rays hit the atmosphere, change from one type to another, proving that they have mass. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald shared the 2015 Nobel Prize for discovering such changes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these elusive particles that interact only through gravity and the weak force.

tossups.p: A detector filled with 1,000 metric tons of heavy water, two kilometers underground in a Canadian nickel mine, showed that these particles from the Sun change type on their way to Earth. Arthur McDonald led that project, called SNO.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny particles produced in huge numbers by fusion in the Sun’s core.

tossups.p: The IceCube observatory uses a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole to detect flashes of light made when these particles strike atoms. In 2018, IceCube traced one of these particles back to a blazar, a distant galaxy with a jet pointed at Earth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ghostly particles that can pass through the entire Earth without stopping.

tossups.p: Leon Lederman, Melvin Schwartz, and Jack Steinberger won a Nobel Prize for showing in 1962 that these particles come in more than one type. The tau type of these particles was first seen directly in 2000 at Fermilab.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electrically neutral particles that Wolfgang Pauli proposed to save the conservation of energy.

tossups.p: Physicists hunt for a rare double beta decay that releases two electrons but none of these particles, which would show that these particles are their own antiparticles. Ettore Majorana [“mah-yoh-RAH-nah”] first suggested that such particles could exist.
tossups.r: They have far less mass than an electron. For 10 points, name these nearly massless particles that stream from the Sun by the trillions.

tossups.p: Detectors for these particles are often built deep underground, in mines or beneath mountains, so that solid rock can block cosmic rays that would swamp their faint signals. These particles travel at nearly the speed of light.
tossups.r: They are given off in beta decay. For 10 points, name these particles, nicknamed “ghost particles,” that rarely interact with matter.

tossups.p: Super-Kamiokande uses about 11,000 light sensors lining a giant tank of ultrapure water to spot rings of Cherenkov [“chuh-REN-kof”] light made when these particles strike the water. These particles are hard to catch because they feel only gravity and the weak force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles that also pour out of nuclear reactors and the Sun.

tossups.p: About 99 percent of the energy released when a massive star’s core collapses in a supernova is carried away by these particles. Huge numbers of these particles are also made by fusion in the Sun’s core.
tossups.r: Trillions of them pass through you every second. For 10 points, name these particles, which have no electric charge and almost no mass.

tossups.p: The MSW effect describes how traveling through dense matter, such as the inside of the Sun, changes the way these particles switch from one type to another. These particles feel only gravity and the weak force, so most pass straight through the whole Earth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ghostly particles that come in electron, muon, and tau flavors and were first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli.

tossups.p: Maurice Goldhaber’s team showed that these particles are always “left-handed,” spinning opposite to the direction they travel. Because these particles have no electric charge, they ignore electromagnetism and pass through matter almost untouched. Pions and muons give off these particles when they decay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles, which Enrico Fermi named with an Italian word meaning “little neutral one.”

clues.t: Nicknamed “ghost particles”: no electric charge, almost no mass, and they barely interact with matter
Trillions from the Sun pass through your body every second without a trace
Given off in radioactive beta decay, along with an electron
Proposed by Wolfgang Pauli (1930); named by Enrico Fermi, Italian for “little neutral one”
Come in three flavors: electron, muon, and tau
Feel only the weak force and gravity, so most pass straight through the whole Earth
First detected in 1956 by Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines near a nuclear reactor
Made in huge numbers by fusion in the Sun’s core
They change flavor as they travel (oscillation), which shows that they have mass
Caught in giant underground tanks of water (Super-Kamiokande in Japan) or in ice at the South Pole (IceCube)
About two dozen from Supernova 1987A were detected, arriving hours before its light; Masatoshi Koshiba shared the 2002 Nobel Prize
Pauli’s 1930 letter, opening “Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen,” called them a “desperate remedy” to save conservation of energy
They are leptons, the neutral partners of the electron, the muon, and the tau
Travel at nearly the speed of light and have far less mass than an electron
Ray Davis’s tank of dry-cleaning fluid in a South Dakota gold mine caught only about a third of the predicted solar ones
John Bahcall calculated how many should come from the Sun; the shortfall puzzled scientists for decades
1998: Super-Kamiokande saw ones from the atmosphere change type; Kajita and McDonald won the 2015 Nobel Prize
SNO, a detector full of heavy water in a Canadian nickel mine, showed that solar ones change type on the way to Earth
OPERA’s 2011 faster-than-light result was traced to a loose fiber-optic cable
Lederman, Schwartz, and Steinberger found the muon type in 1962; the tau type was first seen at Fermilab in 2000
Searches for a double beta decay that gives off two electrons and nothing else test whether they are their own antiparticles (Majorana particles)
Detectors are often built deep underground, in mines or under mountains, so rock blocks out cosmic rays
The MSW effect: traveling through dense matter changes how they switch types
In 2018, IceCube traced one to a blazar, a distant galaxy with a jet pointed at Earth
Carry away about 99 percent of the energy of a collapsing star’s core
Maurice Goldhaber’s team showed they are always “left-handed,” spinning opposite to their motion
Super-Kamiokande’s about 11,000 light sensors watch for rings of Cherenkov light

trap.title: Neutrino or neutron?
trap.body: The names sound alike because Pauli first called his proposed particle a “neutron,” but Enrico Fermi renamed it the neutrino, or “little neutral one,” after James Chadwick discovered the much heavier neutron in 1932. Neutrons sit in the nucleus with protons and are about as heavy as a proton; neutrinos are almost massless and zip through matter at nearly the speed of light. Both have no electric charge, so “neutral” alone won’t tell you which one a tossup wants.
trap.fix: Ghost particles, the missing energy in beta decay, the Sun, oscillation, Super-Kamiokande, or IceCube means neutrinos. The nucleus, Chadwick, neutron stars, or nuclear chain reactions means neutrons.
trap.line: Real answer line: neutrinos (accept specific types like electron neutrinos or antineutrinos; prompt on leptons; do not accept “neutrons”)

topics.name: Magnetic fields
topics.kicker: Invisible zones around magnets and currents · Steer compasses and charges
topics.dates: Linked to electric current by Hans Christian Ørsted, 1820
topics.briefing: A magnetic field is the invisible region around a magnet or an electric current where magnetic forces act. Sprinkle iron filings near a bar magnet and they line up along its field lines, which loop from the north pole around to the south pole. In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying current made a nearby compass needle swing, showing that electricity and magnetism are connected.
topics.answerHtml: magnetic fields (accept B-fields or magnetic flux density; prompt on field or magnetism; do not accept “electric field” or “Earth’s magnetic field”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: George Ellery Hale used the Zeeman effect, the splitting of spectral lines by this quantity, to show in 1908 that sunspots are places where this quantity is very strong. Inside a long coil of wire called a solenoid, this quantity is nearly uniform.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, that iron filings reveal around a bar magnet.

tossups.p: The Biot–Savart [“bee-OH suh-VAR”] law adds up the contributions to this quantity from each tiny piece of a current-carrying wire. Around a long straight wire, this quantity forms circles whose direction is given by a right-hand rule.
tossups.r: Earth has its own version of this quantity. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, that a compass needle lines up with.

tossups.p: In the Meissner [“MYSE-ner”] effect, a superconductor pushes this quantity out of its interior, which lets a small magnet float above the superconductor. Wrapping a current-carrying wire into a coil around an iron nail makes a much stronger version of this quantity, creating an electromagnet.
tossups.r: A compass needle turns to line up with this quantity. For 10 points, name this quantity that surrounds magnets and electric currents.

tossups.p: One of Maxwell’s equations says the divergence of this quantity is always zero, so its lines never start or stop but always form closed loops. Outside a bar magnet, its lines run from the north pole around to the south pole.
tossups.r: No one has ever found a lone north or south pole. For 10 points, name this quantity, whose SI unit is the tesla.

tossups.p: Hall probes measure this quantity by detecting the small voltage that appears across a current-carrying strip placed in it. A charged particle moving through this quantity feels a force at right angles to its motion, so it curves into a circle or spiral.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, that surrounds every magnet and every electric current.

tossups.p: A charged particle circling in this quantity takes the same time for each loop no matter how fast it moves, as long as it is much slower than light, the key idea behind Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron. This quantity never changes a moving charge’s speed, only its direction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, produced by magnets and by moving electric charges.

tossups.p: Inside a long solenoid, this quantity equals the permeability of free space times the current times the number of turns per unit length. Ampère’s law relates this quantity around a closed loop to the current passing through that loop.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which iron filings reveal around a bar magnet.

tossups.p: MRI machines use a very strong version of this quantity to line up the spins of hydrogen nuclei in the body, then use radio waves to make images. Most of those machines produce this quantity with coils of superconducting wire chilled by liquid helium.
tossups.r: Its SI unit, the tesla, is named for the inventor Nikola Tesla. For 10 points, name this quantity that compass needles line up with, found around every magnet.

tossups.p: Magnetars, a kind of neutron star, have the strongest versions of this quantity known in the universe. Earth’s version of this quantity is made by swirling molten iron in its outer core and protects the planet from the solar wind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose lines loop from the north pole to the south pole of a bar magnet.

tossups.p: Mass spectrometers sort ions by bending their paths through this quantity, since lighter ions with the same charge curve more sharply. The Lorentz force law gives the push on a charge moving through this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that Hans Christian Ørsted found an electric current could produce.

tossups.p: Michael Faraday discovered that changing the amount of this quantity passing through a coil of wire creates an electric current, the idea behind electric generators. Lenz’s law says that the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, that surrounds every magnet and can be mapped with iron filings.

tossups.p: Doughnut-shaped machines called tokamaks use this quantity to hold superhot plasma away from their walls in nuclear fusion experiments. Charged particles from the Sun spiral along Earth’s version of this quantity toward the poles, creating auroras.
tossups.r: A compass needle lines up with it. For 10 points, name this quantity, which surrounds both magnets and electric currents.

tossups.p: Magnetotactic bacteria build chains of tiny magnetite crystals that let them line up with Earth’s version of this quantity. Sea turtles and many migrating birds can also sense Earth’s version of this quantity to find their way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas or gauss, that surrounds every magnet.

tossups.p: Superconducting devices called SQUIDs can measure the extremely faint amounts of this quantity produced by electric currents in the human brain. One gauss, an older unit for this quantity, equals one ten-thousandth of a tesla.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that makes a compass needle swing, found around magnets and electric currents.

tossups.p: A pair of Helmholtz coils, spaced one radius apart, creates a nearly uniform region of this quantity between them. A right-hand rule gives the direction of this quantity around a wire: point your thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way this quantity points.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in teslas, that Hans Christian Ørsted showed electric currents produce.

clues.t: The invisible region around a magnet or an electric current where magnetic forces act
Iron filings sprinkled near a bar magnet line up along its lines, which run from the north pole to the south pole
Measured in teslas (named for Nikola Tesla); one tesla equals 10,000 gauss
Compass needles turn to line up with Earth’s version of it
Hans Christian Ørsted (1820) found that an electric current makes one, swinging a nearby compass needle
Symbolized by the letter B; a vector with both a size and a direction
A charge moving through it feels a sideways push (the Lorentz force), so it travels in circles or spirals
Forms circles around a straight current-carrying wire; a right-hand rule gives their direction
Its lines always form closed loops, since no one has found a lone north or south pole (a monopole)
Nearly uniform inside a long coil called a solenoid, where it equals the permeability of free space × turns per unit length × current
Faraday’s law: changing it through a coil makes a current (the idea behind generators); Lenz’s law gives the direction
Earth’s version, made by molten iron in the outer core, steers particles from the Sun toward the poles, making auroras
MRI machines use very strong ones, usually 1.5 or 3 teslas
Does no work on a moving charge: it changes the direction of motion but never the speed
The Zeeman effect: it splits spectral lines; George Ellery Hale used it in 1908 to find strong ones in sunspots
The Biot–Savart law adds up its contributions from each tiny piece of a current
Ampère’s law relates it around a closed loop to the current passing through the loop
The Meissner effect: superconductors push it out, so a small magnet can float above them
Hall probes measure it from the small voltage across a current-carrying strip
A charge circling in it takes the same time per loop at any speed well below light’s, the idea behind Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron
Mass spectrometers sort ions by how sharply it bends their paths
Magnetars, a kind of neutron star, have the strongest ones known in the universe
Tokamaks use it to hold superhot fusion plasma away from their walls
SQUIDs (superconducting quantum interference devices) detect the faint ones made by currents in the brain
Helmholtz coils, spaced one radius apart, make a nearly uniform one between them
Magnetotactic bacteria use magnetite crystals to line up with Earth’s; sea turtles and migrating birds sense it too
Its divergence is always zero, one of Maxwell’s equations (Gauss’s law for magnetism)

trap.title: Magnetic or electric?
trap.body: Electric and magnetic fields are partners (light is a wave of both), so tossups mix their clues, but they are separate answer lines. Magnetic fields come from magnets and moving charges, are measured in teslas, and push only on moving charges, always at right angles to their motion. Questions about the planet’s own field, its flips over time, or the magnetosphere may want “Earth’s magnetic field” instead, so listen for whether the tossup is about Earth or the general idea.
trap.fix: Teslas, gauss, compasses, iron filings, solenoids, the right-hand rule, the Hall effect, or the Zeeman effect means magnetic field. Newtons per coulomb, volts per meter, Coulomb’s law, or the Stark effect means electric field.
trap.line: Real answer line: magnetic fields (accept B-fields or magnetic flux density; prompt on field or magnetism; do not accept “electric field” or “Earth’s magnetic field”)
